_meta.source: MOE admissions pages and school ECG practice
_meta.notes: Player-initiated moves, as opposed to chances, which happen to you. Every move is a real thing a Singapore student can do this year, phrased so a Sec 1 reader could do it tomorrow. EAE and DSA cards checked against moe.gov.sg/post-secondary/admissions/poly-eae and /dsa on the accessed date: Poly EAE is aptitude first and applies in June before results, ITE EAE takes graduating N and O Level students into Higher Nitec, DSA-JC is talent based at Sec 4 and an accepted offer is binding. Two kinds. Asks are superpowers: a held hand of at most three, free to play because asking costs courage rather than time, one a year, and playing one draws another because asking begets knowing who to ask. Commitments consume the year, so they join the turn pool as ordinary choices and spend points; the exchange costs two because three months is three months. Each move sets a flag; some chance cards require those flags, so a move this year changes what can turn up later. That is the point: asking opens things. Moves are bounded to the institution that actually has the role: form teachers, Year Heads and school counsellors end at 17, and post secondary carries its own people, lecturers and career services, then a supervisor at work.

rule: Two kinds. Superpowers are asks: free, held in a hand of five, two a year, and using one teaches you another. Commitments take real time, so they sit among your choices and spend your points.

moves.label: Ask a teacher for help with the subject that scares you
moves.body: Go to the teacher after class. Say which part you do not get. That is the whole move.
moves.outcome: The teacher shows you where it actually went wrong, which is never where you thought.

moves.label: Book a chat with the ECG counsellor
moves.body: Every secondary school and JC has one, and it is free. Bring one question. Where could I go is a good one.
moves.outcome: They show you two roads you did not know existed. Nobody makes you take either.

moves.label: Ask your Year Head what moving up takes
moves.body: Not a promise. A question: what would my marks need to look like to take this at G3?
moves.outcome: Now you know the number. It is smaller than the rumour said.

moves.label: Tell your parents what you actually want
moves.body: They have a plan for you. They cannot compare it with yours if yours stays secret.
moves.outcome: One awkward dinner. After it, one fewer thing to carry alone.

moves.label: Ask for a job shadowing day
moves.body: Your school or a family friend can set one up. One day watching someone actually do the job.
moves.outcome: The job is not what you imagined. Better or worse, now you know which.

moves.label: Start your EAE story
moves.body: Poly and ITE EAE take you on interest and aptitude, before results, in June. They ask what you have made and done. Start having an answer.
moves.outcome: A folder with your name on it: things made, things done, and why this course. Most people start it a week before the deadline. You did not.
moves.check: Poly EAE and ITE EAE, at moe.gov.sg. Applications run in June, before exams.

moves.label: Ask about DSA for JC
moves.body: DSA takes Sec 4s into JC on talent: sport, CCA, a subject you are unusually good at. Fair warning, an accepted offer is binding. You are choosing, not keeping options.
moves.outcome: You find out what your talent area is called on a form. Naming it changes how seriously you take it.
moves.check: DSA for junior colleges, at moe.gov.sg. Accepted offers commit you to that JC.

moves.label: Treat the attachment as the real thing
moves.body: Poly internships and ITE attachments are where employers first see you. Show up like it is the job, because it is.
moves.outcome: Your supervisor writes three sentences about you at the end. People read those.

moves.label: Put your name down for an exchange
moves.body: Poly, ITE and uni all run overseas stints. The form is shorter than the queue for it is.
moves.outcome: Three months somewhere nothing works the way you assume. You come back harder to rattle.

moves.label: Ask a working adult for one hour
moves.body: Find one person doing the thing you want. Ask for an hour and bring questions. Most people say yes and nobody asks them.
moves.outcome: One hour of how it really works, which no website has.

moves.label: Ask your form teacher which subject suits how you learn
moves.body: They see you in class all week. They have an opinion and nobody ever asks for it.
moves.outcome: They name something you are good at that you had not counted as a skill.

moves.label: Talk to a senior who took the road you are curious about
moves.body: One year above you, same school, already there. Ask what they wish they had known.
moves.outcome: Straight answers, no brochure voice. Some of it puts you off, which is also useful.

moves.label: Go to an open house and ask one real question
moves.body: Everyone walks around collecting flyers. Ask a lecturer what students find hardest in year one.
moves.outcome: The answer is specific and nothing like the flyer. You remember it for years.

moves.label: Ask your CCA teacher for something harder
moves.body: Not a bigger title. A real job nobody wants: run the thing, teach the juniors, fix what is broken.
moves.outcome: You are trusted with something before you feel ready, which is how it always goes.

moves.label: Ask someone in your family who took a different road
moves.body: An uncle, a cousin, anyone who did not do what everyone expected. Ask how it worked out.
moves.outcome: Someone in your own family is proof the standard road is not the only one.

moves.label: Ask your lecturer how they got into this
moves.body: Poly and ITE lecturers worked in the trade before they taught it. Most are glad to be asked.
moves.outcome: They tell you the route they actually took, which was not the neat one on the website.

moves.label: Book a session with your school's career services
moves.body: Poly, ITE and every university run one. They know which employers hire from your course, and it is free while you are enrolled.
moves.outcome: They read your resume properly and tell you the two things wrong with it.

moves.label: Ask your supervisor what would get you promoted
moves.body: Not a complaint. A question: what would I need to be doing for this to be the obvious next step?
moves.outcome: They name two things. One you expected. The other you had never thought about.

moves.label: Ask someone whose life you would want how they arranged it
moves.body: Not their job. Their week. How they got the hours to look like that.
moves.outcome: It was arranged on purpose, in steps, and they will tell you the steps if you ask.

moves.label: Ask a younger colleague to teach you something
moves.body: They know the tools you have been avoiding. Asking costs you nothing but the admission.
moves.outcome: Half an hour, and the thing you were dreading turns out to be learnable.

moves.label: Tell the people at home what you are thinking of changing
moves.body: A change at forty lands on everyone you live with. Say it out loud before it is decided.
moves.outcome: They had noticed. Saying it makes it a plan the household is in on, not a surprise.
